newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: SNZ says close to deal with RB on inflation number.
newsitem.headline: SNZ says close to deal with RB on inflation number.

text.p: Government Statistician Len Cook said on Thursday that Statistics New Zealand is close to agreeing with the Reserve Bank over the publication of an underlying inflation rate.
Currently, the Reserve Bank calculates the underlying inflation rate shortly after SNZ publishes the quarterly CPI.
The underlying rate excludes interest rate changes, one-off government charges above a specified level and overseas price shocks.

Cook and Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash on Wednesday briefed key exporter groups who had convened to discuss how the calculation of inflation affected price stability, monetary policy and the exchange rate.
"At the moment we are looking pretty positively at the issue," Cook told Reuters.
SNZ and the RBNZ have discussed the issue over a number of years but failed to agree because of variable factors in the calculation of the underlying rate.
SNZ is currently reviewing the calculation of the CPI with a decision on the review expected at the end of the year.
The exporters recommended at their meeting that SNZ publish the underlying rate to improve the credibility of the data.
The issue of how price shocks are defined remains a sticking point, Cook said.

"We are getting closer and closer to that not being such a big deal. We're not sure whether we are there or not but we are closer than we have ever been. The differences between the organisations' views don't appear to be that dramatic."
Cook expects agreement within a year.
He said SNZ and RBNZ had whittled away most differences over how government charges could be excluded from the calculation of core, or underlying, inflation.
"What has become much more important over time, is the time lag between releasing the CPI and the underlying inflation measure," he said.
Cook said he had strong reservations about the term "underlying inflation".
"If you are subtracting a good number of items from a measure I'm not quite sure what it should be called.
"The Australian one is clearly labelled as 'the Treasury Underlying Inflation Measure'. It is very clearly ascribed to the Australian Treasury," he said.
Cook said the Australian measure removed many items where one-off items could affect the measure and so only included 52 percent of the items in the CPI.
"In New Zealand we don't anticipate changes by reducing items that are volatile, we actually make a direct adjustment.
"It's how you manage to apply judgements to data before you've got them that's been part of our concern."
"But that is less of an issue now than it was a couple of year's ago."
